Active Directory Fundamentals, Forests, Domains and Trusts

 Summary

Active Directory is the object store and trust substrate for almost every Windows network on
earth. Understanding it is not optional for internal work, because everything an attacker does
in AD is a graph traversal — and the graph is defined by objects, groups, sessions and ACLs.

The lecture's framing: AD is not a user database. It is a namespace, a trust boundary
system, and a delegation mechanism. Every misconception about it comes from treating it as a
flat user list.

 Companion to mit858-05 operating systems and tcm-06's trust-path
 section. This note is the substrate; ad-02 is the protocol on top.

 The objects

  GROUP             a collection of principals, used for authorisation
  COMPUTER          a machine account; a USER with a $ in the name
  ORGANIZATIONAL UNIT OU  a container for delegation of administration
  DOMAIN            the security boundary; a database NTDS.dit + a set of servers
  FOREST            the top of the hierarchy; a security boundary of last resort
  GLOBAL CATALOG    a read-only, forest-wide index, replicated to e

Kerberos Deep Dive: TGTs, Service Tickets and Delegation

 Summary

Kerberos is three ideas: a ticket that lets you prove who you are without sending a password,
a referral that tells you where to get one, and delegation that lets a service act on
your behalf. Every AD attack in this course is one of those three being abused.

The lecture's framing: a ticket is a bearer credential. Whoever holds it
can use it. That single property explains Kerberoasting, delegation,
ticket theft, and why the ticket lifetime is the security parameter.

 The three objects

    the long-term secret, derived from the account PASSWORD and the REALM
    AES: PBKDF2password, salt=REALMUPPER, iterations
    the KDC has it; the user could compute it; a DC can decrypt with it
     This is why roasting a ticket is cracking a password. <<<

    issued by the Authentication Service to a user
    encrypted with the KDC's own long-term key
    contains: identity, groups, session key, validity
    THIS IS THE CROWN JEWEL. One TGT = the user. Everything after it

LDAP Enumeration and BloodHound Graph Analysis

 Summary

LDAP is the interface to the directory, and it is almost entirely unauthenticated-readable by
default. That is the single most important fact about AD reconnaissance: the majority of the
attack surface can be enumerated with no credentials at all.

The lecture's structure: what LDAP lets you ask anonymously, what it lets
you ask with a user, and why the graph derived from those answers is
what makes AD attacks tractable at all.

 LDAP as a query language

text
  EVERY OBJECT has a DN, a set of attributes, and a class.

  FILTER syntax RFC 4515:
    &objectClass=useruserAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=512
      AND   objectClass=user
      AND   userAccountControl has bit 512 set normal account
              ^ "userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803" is the
                extensible match for "bitwise AND contains value"

  KEY BIT VALUES in userAccountControl - you will see these constantly:
    0x0002  ACCOUNTDISABLE

Windows Privilege Escalation and GPO Abuse

 Summary

Domain admin is rarely the goal — local admin on a useful host is. This note is the Windows
escalation catalogue: the misconfigurations that turn a user into an administrator, and the
Group Policy mechanism that turns one admin into domain admin without touching a single host.

GPO abuse is the part that surprises people: it is a domain-wide escalation executed
through an ordinary management tool, with no exploit and often no host access at all.

 Companion to ex-01..ex-06 the exploitation mechanics and ad-03's
 graph. This note is the Windows-specific escalation and the GPO abuse.

 Local escalation: the catalogue

text

    C:\Program Files\My App\ - the space is the vulnerability
    writable service binary
    service with a weak DACL on the binary or its directory
    DLL search order hijack on a service that loads from a writable path
    unquoted path + writable C:\ - plant the exe

  FILE PERMISSIONS
    a user-writable directory on the PATH of a service
    a user-writable scheduled task file

Cryptography I: Introduction, IND-CPA

 Summary

CS161's crypto block starts where MIT 6.858's does: with a definition. Before you can say
an encryption scheme is secure, you must write down what "secure" means and prove the scheme
achieves it.

 Companion to cry-01..cry-07 and mit858-13. This note is the formal
 foundation; those are the practical applications.

 Semantic security IND-CPA

The definition that replaced "the ciphertext looks random":

text
An encryption scheme is IND-CPA secure if, for any PPT adversary A:

  1.  A submits two messages m0, m1
  2.  A receives Enck, mb for a uniformly random b ∈ {0,1}
  3.  A outputs b'

  AdvA = |Prb' = b - 1/2|

  A is broken if AdvA is non-negligible  1/polyλ for some polynomial


The intuition: an eavesdropper learns nothing about which of two
messages was encrypted. Not "the plaintext is hard to recover" — nothing at
all, not even partial information.

Why it matters: IND-CPA rules out every cipher that leaks any function
of the plaintext. ECB fails it visibly. A stream cipher with a reused nonce
fails it catastrophically. XOR with a fixed pad fails it trivially.

b:
Memory Safety and Buffer Overflows

 Summary

CS161's memory-safety block is the formal counterpart to MIT 6.858's Lab 1. Same bug class, but
presented as a language problem with a taxonomy, which is what makes the fix structural rather
than defensive.

 Companion to mit858-04 and ex-01..ex-06. This note is the taxonomy and
 the language argument; those are the exploitation mechanics.

 The taxonomy

CS161 groups memory-safety bugs into five families. Knowing the list is most
of knowing what to look for.

| Bug | Definition | Typical consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Buffer overflow | Write/read outside a fixed-size buffer | Overwrite adjacent memory |
| Integer overflow | Arithmetic wraps past a type's bound | Wrong size, wrong index, undersized allocation |
| Use after free | Reference memory after it was released | Dangling pointer, type confusion |
| Uninitialized memory | Read memory never written | Information disclosure |
| Type confusion | Treat one type as another | Arbitrary read/write via mismatched layout |

They are not independent. Integer overflow causes most heap bugs: an
int size computation wraps, an allocation is too small, and the
subsequent write is an overflow.

OS Security: Privilege Separation

 Summary

CS161's OS-security block asks how an operating system stays trustworthy while running thousands
of untrusted programs. The lecture's answer is the same one MIT 6.858 reaches, stated as a
design requirement rather than an architecture: the OS must be the only thing you trust, and it
must therefore be as small as it can be.

 Companion to mit858-02 and mit858-05. This note is the threat model
 against the kernel; those are the mechanisms.

 The adversary, precisely

An operating system faces adversaries it cannot trust:

text
  ordinary processes   - run arbitrary code, deliberately buggy or malicious
  users               - may attempt to read others' data, escalate
  input               - network data reaching a parser
  the hardware         - assume honest
  the OS itself        - if it is compromised, everything is lost


The design goal: a compromise of any userland component must not yield
kernel privilege, because privilege is what the kernel holds.

Network Security and Firewalls

 Summary

CS161 treats the network as hostile by assumption and asks what security is possible at each
layer. The lecture's conclusion is that almost nothing is possible below the transport layer
without cryptography, and firewalls are a policy control rather than a security control.

 Companion to ccna-01..ccna-08 and mit858-12. Those teach the
 protocols; this note is about what a filter can and cannot achieve.

 What a firewall can do

A packet filter makes a decision per packet or per flow on a tuple:

text
  src IP, dst IP, src port, dst port, protocol, flags, interface, direction


Actions: allow, deny, reject, log, rate-limit, or reset the connection.

That is the entire expressive power of a stateless filter. It cannot
know who the user is, what the data contains, or whether the request is
authorised. It is an access control list over packets.

| | Stateless | Stateful |
|---|---|---|
| Decisions on | each packet independently | connection state |
| Example | ip6tables | iptables -m conntrack, nftables |
| Knows "is this a reply?" | no | yes |
| Can permit replies | no — you must write an inbound rule | yes |

 Summary

Transport layer: ports, connection state, reliability. This lecture is where scanning becomes
predictable, because nmap's scan types and every network service's behaviour are direct
consequences of how TCP establishes, uses, and tears down a connection.

 Key ideas

- Three-way handshake: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK. This is why state exists and why SYN scanning works
- Four-way FIN teardown, RST for immediate abort
- Half-open: a SYN scan never completes the handshake, so the server logs little
- Sequence numbers: 32-bit, per-direction. The basis of TCP sequence prediction attacks
- UDP has no handshake — no state, no guarantee. Scanning UDP is slow and unreliable
- Ports: 0-1023 well-known, 1024-49151 registered, 49152-65535 ephemeral

 Summary

Before you exploit anything you must know what is protecting it. checksec reads a binary and
tells you which mitigations are compiled in. That report dictates your technique — there is no
point writing shellcode for a binary with NX enabled.

Every exploit starts with this file.

 Key ideas

- NX: the stack and heap are not executable. Shellcode must be read in, or you must ROP
- PIE: the binary loads at a random base. You need an address leak
- Stack canary: a random value between locals and the return address. Corrupt it and the
  program aborts before returning
- RELRO: makes the GOT read-only after relocation. Full RELRO closes the GOT-overwrite route
- ASLR is not a binary flag — it is a system-wide runtime setting
- Compile flags let you turn each mitigation off, which is exactly what exploit courses do

|---|---|---|---|
| Stack canary | -fno-stack-protector | checksec → "Stack canary: found" |  stack smashing detected  and SIGABRT |
| NX | -z execstack | GNUSTACK RWX | cannot jump to address on stack from your she

 Summary

Before you can overwrite a return address you must know exactly where it is relative to your
buffer. This lecture produces those numbers by measurement rather than by calculation, because
the compiler inserts padding you will not have predicted.

 Key ideas

- x86-64 System V ABI: push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp,N on entry
- Locals sit at lower addresses than the saved RBP and return address
- The stack grows downward, so overflowing a buffer walks upward toward ret
- 16-byte stack alignment is enforced, so the offset is rarely a round number
- Measure rbp - rsp and the frame contents; do not compute and hope
- Record the numbers in your scratchpad; every later exercise needs them

│ arg1 arg1            │

  └─ address of system in libc

b:
Bypassing NX, PIE and Full RELRO

 Summary

The final board. With NX on, PIE on, and Full RELRO, most of the classic routes are closed. What
remains is a set of specific, well-understood techniques — and the recognition that a hardened
binary often is not the right target.

 Key ideas

- NX: return to existing code ROP, ret2libc, or place shellcode somewhere executable and jump
- PIE: leak the binary base or a libc pointer from a format string or an uninitialised read
- Full RELRO: GOT is read-only → target mallochook/freehook older glibc, the
  exit handlers, a .finiarray entry, or overwrite a live function pointer
- Modern glibc 2.34+ removed mallochook/freehook — use environ, TLS, or FSOP
- Stack pivot: move RSP to a larger writable region to gain more overflow capacity
- JOP / SROP: when you cannot find a usable chain in the binary
- The honest answer: a properly hardened binary is not the way in. Look for a weaker service.

 The hardened binary's attack surface

| Mitigation | Closed off | What is still open |
|---|---|---|
| NX | Stack shellcode | ROP, ret2libc, writable+executable regions JIT, ld.so |
| PIE | Fixed code addresses | Info leaks, partial over-reads, uninitialis

Every file system loses data. A file that is deleted leaves its content on the disk until
overwritten. The discipline is knowing where data can hide — in slack space, in unallocated
clusters, in alternate data streams, inside other files — and how to extract it without corrupting
the evidence.

The framing: the file system's view of a file is not the only view of
its bytes. NTFS has slack, streams, and resident data; a PNG can
contain an entire ZIP; an email client stores attachments in its own
format.

      clusters freed by a deletion, before anything reused them.
      The richest source of deleted files, and the first thing

Your first real tool run. We will scan 127.0.0.1 — your own machine, where there is no legal

nmap sends a probe and classifies the response:

| Response | Meaning |

| SYN / SYN,ACK | Port open, something is listening |
| RST | Port closed, host is up |

Kali Linux is a rolling, Debian-derived Linux distribution built by and for people who
do security testing. Three words in that sentence matter more than the rest.

b:
Your First Session: Terminal, User, and HOME

 Summary

Your first interactive session on a Linux machine is a conversation between three parties: you
the shell, reading what you type, the shell a program that interprets your line and asks
the kernel to do things, and the kernel which owns the hardware and decides what is allowed.

Almost every "this doesn't work" moment on a new Linux install traces back to a misunderstanding
about which of those three is responsible for what.

 The three-layer model


   you type:  ls -la /etc
        ↓
   SHELL      reads the line, splits it into words, expands globs and variables,
              finds ls on PATH, waits for it to finish
        ↓
   KERNEL     resolves the path, opens files, reads directories, enforces permissions
        ↓
   HARDWARE   the disk


The practical consequence: when a command does not exist, that is the shell's problem. When a
command runs and gives "Permission denied", that is the kernel's problem. Knowing which layer
is complaining tells you where to look.

 Your identity on the machine

id             uid=1000nwpcs gid=1000nwpcs groups=1000nwpcs,27sudo,...
echo $HOME     /home/nwpcs

navigable. Every tool in this curriculum is a binary in /usr/bin, but the interesting parts

directories that have a consistent, learnable layout.

This is the single highest-value five minutes of orientation you will spend on Kali.

 Summary

Kali is a rolling release: there is no version to upgrade to, only a repository that is
always in motion. apt update && apt upgrade on Kali can change thousands of packages across a
few hundred megabytes and — because Kali tracks upstream quickly — can occasionally leave you with
a mismatched library that breaks one tool.

This is the most common way new Kali users lose their environment. This lecture is about doing it
safely.

 How a rolling upgrade actually differs from Debian

| | Debian stable | Kali rolling |
|---|---|---|
| Upgrade size | Occasionally large, then quiet for months | Potentially large any day |
| Library versions | Frozen for the release lifetime | Track upstream within days |
| apt upgrade | Safe, predictable | Usually safe; occasionally a tool breaks |
| Risk | Very low | Low, but non-zero and hard to predict |
| Recovery | Install an older ISO | Restore a snapshot or rollback |

- The directory matters, not just the file. A writable directory containing an executable

- PATH hijacking: if any PATH directory is writable by your user, you control that command
- Unsafe interpreter calls: system"sh -c 'input'" runs sh from PATH

b:

 Summary

A kernel exploit is the last resort, not the first. This lecture covers when it is justified, how
the privilege-escalation decision tree actually works, and how to study Dirty Pipe as the
canonical modern walkthrough.

 Key ideas

- Escalation order: credentials → misconfiguration → SUID/service abuse → PATH/cron →

- Kernel exploit preconditions: a known local privilege boundary to cross. If you are already
  root, there is nothing to escalate.
- Finding a kernel bug: uname -r → identify version → searchsploit linux kernel <version
  → check for a local privesc PoC
- Dirty Pipe CVE-2022-0847: an arbitrary write to the page cache as root, and the cleanest
  modern kernel exploit to study
- Modern kernels restrict unprivileged user namespaces, which breaks many published privesc
  chains — you must check, not assume

s: x86-64 Assembly and Reverse Engineering - T03
b:
Binary, Hex and the CPU Fetch-Execute Cycle

 Summary

Everything a computer does is a number being moved and transformed. Before any of the higher
level work — reverse engineering, exploitation, protocol analysis — you need the fetch-execute
cycle to be automatic rather than something you have to think about.

The content here is the foundation: how a number is represented, how the CPU reads bytes, and
why that makes hex the native language of the field.

 Everything is bits; we group them

text
  1 bit   0 or 1
  8 bits  1 byte    - 0x00 .. 0xFF    256 values
  16 bits 2 bytes   - uint16           65,536 values
  32 bits 4 bytes   - uint32           4,294,967,296 values
  64 bits 8 bytes   - uint64, pointer  1.8 x 10^19 values

  hex digit = 4 bits   -  one hex digit is exactly half a byte
  hex byte  = 2 digits -  0x41 is 0100 0001


Hex exists because binary grouping is unreadable and base 16 maps exactly onto nibbles. There
is no arithmetic in hex; it is a display convenience. 0x41 is the same as 65, which is the
same as 'A'.

 Signed numbers, and why it matters for overflow

text
  int8:   0x7F = 127        0x80 = -128      two's complement
  int32:  0x7FFFFFFF = 2147483647

gdb is not a debugger that happens to show assembly. It is a control-flow instrument: you
stop the program wherever you want, look at every piece of state, and step one instruction at
a time. That is the difference between guessing at a binary and knowing.

The skill is not memorising commands. It is knowing how to answer four
questions about any function you have never seen.

 Companion to lo-03 instructions and lo-04 the format. This note

 The four questions

text
  For any function you have never seen, you need:

  2. WHAT DOES IT TRUST?    which inputs are validated, which are not
  3. WHERE DOES IT JUMP?    branches, calls, and especially indirect ones
  4. WHAT CAN I CORRUPT?    which of its inputs reach a dangerous sink

  gdb answers 1 and 4 directly. Static analysis answers 2 and 3.
  You need both, and the combination is much faster than either.

  BREAKPOINT                   stop when an address is reached

Lecture 1 of 6.858 sets the frame for everything else: what is being protected, from whom, and
why. The central move is separating assets, adversaries and security goals before
discussing a single mechanism.

 Key ideas

- A threat model answers: who are we defending against, what do they want, what can they do?
- Assets are what matter; security effort is spent in proportion to their value
- Adversaries differ in capability enormously — an end user, a malicious process, a
  compromised kernel, the vendor, a network attacker
- Security goals: confidentiality, integrity, availability, plus correctness and
  accountability
- Attacker-controlled input is the root of most vulnerabilities: untrusted data reaching a
  trusted computation
- The lecture's running example: a web server that crashes on malformed input is a vulnerability
  even if you do not yet know how to exploit it

 The frame: assets, adversaries, goals

| Adversary | Capability | Realistic goal |
|---|---|---|
| Remote user | Send crafted requests | Code execution on the server |
| Malicious app | Run code as the user | Read other users' files, escalate |

Security Architecture

 Summary

Lecture 2 covers the structural question: where do you put the trust boundary, and how do you
make the trusted part small enough to audit?

The answer the lecture develops is privilege separation — splitting a large untrusted program
into a small trusted monitor plus a large unprivileged userland.

 Key ideas

- Minimize the trusted computing base: everything that must be correct for security to hold
- Privilege separation: split into a small privileged monitor and untrusted userland
- Application-level vs OS-level: Linux namespaces, chroot, VMs are different layers of the
  same idea
- Security vs reliability: privileged code must be simple, because it cannot recover
- Sandboxing: restrict a process without trusting it
- Reference monitors: the component that mediates every privileged operation

 The privilege separation pattern

   │  unprivileged userland       │  large, complex, crashable
   │  parser, renderer, network   │  bugs here are survivable
   └───────────┬──────────────────┘

The lecture's own reading is telling: Your password doesn't matter.

- Authentication who is separate from authorisation what
- Three factors: something you know, something you have, something you are
- Passwords fail because of reuse, phishing, and poor storage, not because they are weak math
- Offline attackability is the property that matters: can the verifier be attacked at leisure?
  Password hashes: yes. Biometrics: yes. Online-attempt-limited factors: harder
- Session handling is where authentication actually breaks
- Second factors work when the second factor is not also phishable or replayable
- Trust recovery and account recovery are security functions, not UX details

1. Users reuse them across sites → one breach unlocks many
2. They are phishable → a look-alike login page captures them
3. They are typed on compromised machines → keyloggers

Privilege Separation

 Summary

If you cannot make the trusted code small, split it. Put a small privileged component in front
of a large unprivileged one, so that a bug in the large part costs you the large part rather than
the system.

The lecture's reading is OKWS O'Keefe et al., which is the canonical description of this
pattern.

 Key ideas

- Privilege separation: privileged monitor + unprivileged userland
- The monitor owns the resources; userland does the work
- The interface between them is a small message protocol — and every message must be validated
- Goals: survive crashes in userland, limit the blast radius of a bug, enable review
- The classic case: Postfix, and the split between a privileged master and unprivileged
  helper processes
- Failure mode: a validation bug in the monitor, or a confused deputy where userland convinces
  the monitor to do something it should not

 The shape

      network

If a bug in one component must not compromise the whole system, isolate the component. This

 Key ideas

- Isolation vs sandboxing: isolation is the mechanism; sandboxing is a policy applied with it
- Language-level sandboxing: the runtime enforces memory safety, so a bug stays in-process

- Native Client NaCl/Sandboxing API: a restricted instruction subset with validation
- Hypervisors: Type 1 bare metal, e.g. Xen and Type 2 hosted, e.g. VirtualBox/KVM
- Static binary verification: measure the code at load time and refuse to run if changed
- The trade: isolation costs performance and memory, and every new interface is new code

Enclaves

 Summary

Process isolation asks the kernel for help. Trust-based isolation asks the CPU instead. An
enclave Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone is a region of memory the CPU itself encrypts and
protects, with entry and exit measured by the hardware.

This is the lecture's answer to: what if the OS itself is the adversary?

 Key ideas

- Trusted Execution Environments TEEs: hardware-isolated regions with measured entry
- SGX: enclaves in unencrypted normal memory, encrypted while resident; keys derived from
  measured code
- Launch / measurement: a trusted computing base hashes the code before launch; that hash is
  the identity
- Remote attestation: prove to a third party what code is running inside the enclave
- TrustZone: an ARM secure world, a whole OS, hardware isolated
- The catch: the CPU has to decrypt into memory, so side channels become the attack

Symbolic Execution

 Summary

Testing every input is impossible; reasoning about paths is not. Symbolic execution executes
a program with symbolic rather than concrete inputs, so each branch forks into both possibilities
and the tool tracks the set of states that could reach your target.

This is MIT 6.858 lecture 10, and the practical reading is on symbolic execution finding "inputs
of death" in real binaries.

 Key ideas

- Replace concrete values with symbolic ones; the program forks at each branch
- Maintain a path condition: the constraints that must hold to reach this state
- Goal-directed search: keep only states that can still reach the target
- Concrete execution run it for real versus concrete symbolic execution fork the
  uninteresting parts, run the interesting ones
- Fuzzers AFL do the opposite: random inputs with coverage feedback. Symbolic goes
  exhaustively; fuzzing goes broad and cheap. They are complements.
- The limit is path explosion: 100 branches = 2^100 paths

- IP is unauthenticated and unauthenticable: source addresses are claimed, not proven

- Key agreement Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret without transmitting it
- Authentication is the hard part: DH alone is vulnerable to a man in the middle
- Signatures and certificates bind an identity to a key
- Forward secrecy: compromise of the long-term key must not decrypt old traffic
- Ephemeral DH: a fresh key pair per session, which is what buys forward secrecy
- The transcript matters: everything exchanged is authenticated, including the handshake itself
- The lecture's preparation reading is the SSL 3.0 analysis Joux, which is why TLS 1.3 removed

A certificate says: this public key belongs to this name, and I, a certificate authority, vouch

- Chain of trust: leaf → intermediate → root, each signing the one below
- A browser ships a root store; the chain terminates there
- Validation must check: chain to a trusted root, name match, validity dates, revocation,

- Name matching has been a rich source of bugs: wildcards, null bytes in CN, IDN

- Revocation barely works in practice OCSP stapling, CRLs — browsers soft-fail
- Compromised CAs are the catastrophic failure: one rogue CA can forge any certificate
- Certificate pinning reduces reliance on the public PKI

A client MUST check, before trusting a certificate:

Lecture 18 is the capstone: an attacker with no bug to exploit, no key to steal, and often no

- Side channels: secrets leak through time, cache state, power, or contention

- Speculative execution: the CPU executes past a bounds check or a permission check, and the

- Meltdown: speculative read of kernel memory, then a fault; flush+reload recovers it
- Spectre: speculative execution poisons a branch predictor or a register

- The lesson: physical properties become security properties once data depends on them

1. a secret-dependent operation
2. an observable side effect of that operation
3. the ability to measure the side effect

Isolation Mechanisms

 Summary

Isolation is the OS's core security service: ensuring one entity cannot read, corrupt, or control
another. It comes in layers, and each layer can fail in its own way.

- Address space isolation — separate virtual memory per process
- Mode protection — kernel/user rings
- Privilege separation — trusted monitor, untrusted userland
- Sandboxing — restrict what a program may do
- Objects and capabilities — make authority explicit and transferable

A single layer is not enough. The Linux design "everything is a process" is what makes this
tractable: if a component must be trusted, it is a small, isolated process rather than a
privileged function in a big binary.

Each process gets its own virtual address space. The MMU translates virtual to physical
addresses on demand, and the page table defines what is legal.

Process A  0x400000..0x600000 - its own pages
Process B  0x400000..0x600000 - completely different physical pages


The same virtual address in two processes means nothing to each other. This is why
ASLR and stack overflows coexist: if you know an address, you can write to it — ASLR only
raises the cost of guessing.

- Isolation: process A cannot touch process B's pages
- Abstraction: programs see a linear address space regardless of physical layout
- Efficiency: swap, demand paging, copy-on-write
- Protection: NX no execute, user/supervisor bit per page

MIT's The Missing Semester of Your CS Education exists because every computer science degree

Shell Tools & Scripting

 Summary

Tools become weapons when you chain them. The shell's real power is that every tool's stdout is
data, and you can pipe that into the next tool's stdin. A human reading a 400-line nmap scan
takes minutes; a well-written pipeline extracts the three facts that matter in one second.

This is also where shell scripting stops being optional: reconnaissance automation, evidence
collection, and every tool invocation you will script later.

 The six tools that cover 90% of shell work

| Tool | Job | Think of it as |
|---|---|---|
| grep | select lines | SQL WHERE |
| cut / awk | select columns | SELECT col |
| sort / uniq | order and dedupe | ORDER BY, DISTINCT |
| head / tail | limit rows | LIMIT |
| sed | substitute / transform | UPDATE |
| xargs | parallelise | a for loop that respects spaces |

echo "$V"       "hello world"   <- expansion happens

The Command Line Environment

 Summary

This lecture covers the environment a command runs inside: which directories the shell searches
PATH, which variables it exports, and how to make settings persist. Three tools dominate:
~/.bashrc, ~/.profile, and /etc/environment.

It sounds mundane. It is also where several real attack paths live — an attacker who can append
one line to your ~/.bashrc has persistence; a script that trusts $PATH can be hijacked; and
LDPRELOAD turns any non-setuid program into your program.

 PATH: the search order

When you type nmap, the shell checks each $PATH directory left to right, in order, and
runs the first match. Consequences:

bash
echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | nl

 Which one wins if there are two?
type -a nmap

 Proof of concept: hijack a command with a directory earlier in PATH
mkdir -p /tmp/evil
printf '!/bin/sh\necho "you just ran MY ls, not /bin/ls"\n'  /tmp/evil/ls
chmod +x /tmp/evil/ls
PATH=/tmp/evil:$PATH ls -la       yes, that works, and it is a real technique


Defence: never put a writable directory early in PATH, and always invoke tools by absolute
path /usr/bin/passwd, not passwd in security-critical scripts. /usr/local/sbin and

 Summary

Software is built by programs, not people. Build systems turn source into artefacts in a
repeatable way, and dependency managers fetch and pin the libraries your build needs.

For a security student this is not busywork. Three concrete reasons:

1. You will compile vulnerable programs Tier 3 and need to know which flags disable which

3. Reproducibility is a professional skill. "It worked on my machine" is not acceptable
   when you hand someone a tool.

t: Network Models, OSI and TCP/IP Stacks
b:
Network Models, OSI and TCP/IP Stacks

 Summary

The theoretical layer stack, with the Neso-style emphasis on what each layer is responsible for
and why the layering exists at all.

 Key ideas

- Layering gives independent evolution: change Wi-Fi without rewriting TCP
- Each layer provides a service to the one above and uses the one below
- Peer-to-peer communication between layers on different hosts is an illusion — the bytes
  always traverse the whole stack on both sides
- Encapsulation on send, decapsulation on receive
- No layer may skip or reorder — that constraint is why HTTP cannot sit directly on Ethernet
  even when it theoretically could

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Layer / layer 7 | A level of abstraction in the protocol stack |
| Service primitive | The operation a layer offers upward |
| Peer protocol | The same layer talking across the network |
| Encapsulation / decapsulation | Adding / removing headers |
| PDU | Protocol data unit at that layer |
| Multiplexing | Several higher-layer flows sharing one lower-layer flow |
| Service data unit | The data a service passes up |
| Peer-to-peer | Logical communication between equal layers on different host

t: Data Link Layer: Framing, MAC, Error Control
b:
Data Link Layer: Framing, MAC, Error Control

 Summary

How bits become frames, how frames find their destination, and how errors are detected. Layer 2
is where the first security boundary of any network appears — and where the first attack surface
does too.

 Key ideas

- Framing: delimiters, addresses, type/length, payload, FCS
- MAC addressing is flat: every node listens to every frame. No hierarchy, no broadcast
  control. That single property enables ARP poisoning and MAC flooding
- Error control: CRC/FCS detects corruption but does not correct; the frame is simply dropped
- Flow control: not really present in shared Ethernet; collision handling came with CSMA/CD
- Switching replaced the collision domain problem but kept the broadcast domain intact
- Promiscuous mode is what a sniffer needs, and why a switched network does not help you

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Frame | The Layer 2 unit with a header and FCS |
| FCS / CRC | Frame Check Sequence; detects, does not repair |
| CSMA/CD | Carrier sense with collision detection; historical |
| Promiscuous mode | Accept every frame, not just your own |
| MTU | Largest frame payload a link carries |
| NIC | The netw

MAC Protocols, CSMA/CD and Switching

 Summary

How a shared medium became a switched one, and the attack surface each stage introduced.

 Key ideas

- CSMA/CD: listen, transmit, detect collision, back off exponentially. Historical — switched
  Ethernet made it unnecessary
- Collision domain: a hub shares one; a switch gives one per port; full duplex removes it
- Broadcast domain: unchanged by switching; only routers and VLANs split it
- Store-and-forward vs cut-through trade latency for reliability
- STP/RSTP prevents loops, and its own design creates a well-known hijack opportunity
- Port security, MAC limits and DHCP snooping exist because the Layer 2 threat model is weak

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| CSMA/CD | Carrier sense multiple access with collision detection |
| Backoff | Exponential random wait after a collision |
| Collision domain | Where frames can collide |
| Broadcast domain | Where broadcasts propagate |
| Store-and-forward | Buffer the whole frame before forwarding |
| Cut-through | Forward as soon as the destination is known |
| STP / RSTP | Spanning tree; prevents switching loops |

Network Layer: IP, Subnetting, Routing

 Summary

The network layer's job is to move packets between networks. Its central design decision —
a connectionless, best-effort, header-based forwarding model — is exactly why it is the most
abused layer in security.

 Key ideas

- IP is connectionless: no setup, no acknowledgement, no guarantee of delivery or order
- Best effort: packets may be dropped, duplicated, reordered, or corrupted in transit
- Routing is per-hop: each router decides independently using longest-prefix match
- Decentralised control is the internet's strength and its security weakness: no authority
  can revoke a spoofed source address, because nobody checks
- Fragmentation happens here; a router that needs to fragment and cannot decrements TTL and
  sends ICMP "frag needed"
- IPv4 header fields that matter: TTL, protocol, source, destination, options which can
  hide data

|---|---|

| Best effort | No delivery guarantee |
| Hop-by-hop | Decided independently at each router |

- TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled, stateful
- UDP: connectionless, no guarantees, 8-byte header, used by DNS, DHCP, QUIC
- Sockets are the kernel objects; every flow is one
- Port states LISTEN, SYNSENT, ESTABLISHED, TIMEWAIT are what you read when diagnosing
- Well-known vs ephemeral: knowing the range tells you whether a port is a service or a

t: Basics of OS: Computer System Operation & Storage Structure
b:
Basics of OS: Computer System Operation & Storage Structure

 Summary

Before algorithms and scheduling, a Neso-style foundation lecture: what a computer is made of,
what an OS manages, and how storage is structured. Security-relevant conclusions arrive
immediately — the OS is the trusted intermediary on every trust boundary you test later.

 Key ideas

- Hardware: CPU registers, ALU, control unit, memory hierarchy registers → cache → RAM →
  disk, I/O devices, buses.
- OS as resource manager: decides who gets the CPU, how much memory, which device.
- OS as virtual machine: provides an abstract machine files, processes, sockets so programs
  do not touch hardware directly.
- Memory hierarchy: the reason caching exists, and the reason cache timing is a side channel.
- Storage structure: registers → cache → main memory → secondary storage. Each is a
  performance layer with a different trust story.

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ALU | Arithmetic logic unit; performs operations |
| Register | Fastest, smallest CPU storage |
| Cache | Small fast memory, hierarchy between CPU and RAM |
| DMA | Direct memory access; devices bypass the CPU |
| System call | Program → kernel

I/O Structure and System Calls

 Summary

How a program actually gets bytes from a device to itself, and where the OS inserts itself. The
I/O path is the most security-relevant path in any system: every byte a web server serves and
every packet a sniffer reads passed through it.

 Key ideas

- Programmed I/O — CPU polls the device. Slow, simple.
- Interrupt-driven I/O — device raises an interrupt; CPU handles it later. The standard model.
- DMA — device writes directly to RAM; CPU is interrupted only at completion.
- Spooling — a daemon holds a device exclusively printer, serialising access.
- The I/O path: device → driver → buffer → kernel → syscall → user buffer.
- Why it matters: buffer sizes, TOCTOU on device files, and /dev/ permissions are all
  attack surface.

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Driver | Kernel code controlling one device class |
| Interrupt | Signal from device asking for CPU attention |
| DMA | Direct memory access, bypassing CPU |
| Buffering | Absorbing speed differences between device and CPU |
| Spooling | Daemon-owned exclusive device access |
| Device file | /dev/ node used to talk to a driver |
| /dev/shm | Shared memory tmpfs |
| ioctl |

Processes, Threads and Process Control

 Summary

A process is an executing program with its own resources: address space, open files, credentials.
Threads share everything except the stack and registers.

Security-wise, a process is the unit of isolation and a thread is the unit of shared risk.
Getting this distinction right explains privilege boundaries, ptrace targets, and why memory
corruption in a multithreaded server is catastrophic.

 Key ideas

- Process states: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated.
- Process Control Block PCB: PID, state, PC, registers, memory info, open files, credentials.
- Program vs process: a program on disk is not running; the process is the instance.
- Threads: shared heap, shared files, per-thread stack.
- fork: duplicates the address space copy-on-write.
- execve: replaces the image entirely — a different program in the same PID.
- Zombie: exited process whose parent has not reaped it.
- Credentials live per-process: which is why setuid binaries matter.

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| PID | Process identifier |
| PCB | Kernel's per-process record |
| fork | Create a child process |
| execve | Replace the current program image |
|

Scheduling and Synchronisation

 Summary

Scheduling decides who runs next. Synchronisation decides how concurrent entities cooperate
without corrupting each other's data. Both are security-relevant: a bad scheduler is a
denial-of-service vector, and bad synchronisation is a data race.

 Key ideas

- Scheduling criteria: turnaround, throughput, fairness, response time, priority.
- Preemptive vs non-preemptive: can the OS interrupt a running process?
- FCFS — simple, unfair convoy effect. SJF — optimal average, starves long jobs.
  Round robin — a time slice each. Priority — nice, but needs ageing to avoid starvation.
- Multilevel feedback queues: approximate SJF adaptively without knowing burst times.
- Synchronisation: mutexes, semaphores, monitors, condition variables.
- Producer/consumer — the canonical shared-buffer problem.
- Deadlock: hold-and-wait, mutual exclusion, no preemption, circular wait.

Security connection: starvation and unfair scheduling are DoS; races are exploitable races.

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Preemption | OS forcibly interrupting a running process |
| Time slice / quantum | How long a process runs before switching |
| FCFS | First come

Deadlocks and Classical Problems

 Summary

Synchronisation has an inherent tension: you cannot have both maximum concurrency and freedom
from deadlock. The classical problems producers/consumers, readers/writers, dining philosophers
are the minimal cases where that tension is visible.

Security relevance: deadlocks are denial of service with no attacker required; starvation is a
DoS an attacker can induce deliberately.

 Key ideas

- Producer/consumer: bounded buffer. Needs mutual exclusion no corruption plus
  synchronisation no over/under-run. Solved with two semaphores and a mutex.
- Readers/writers: many concurrent readers, exclusive writers. Solutions: reader preference
  starves writers, writer preference starves readers, fair FIFO — each costs something.
- Dining philosophers: five philosophers, five forks. Naive solutions deadlock or starve.
  Solutions: ordering the forks by number, limiting four philosophers, or the waiter/arbitrator
  pattern.
- The general lesson: every synchronisation policy is a fairness policy, and fairness is
  always a trade.

 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Bounded buffer | Fixed-size shared queue |
| Readers/writers | Shared resourc

t: Bandit Levels 0-10: SSH, ls, find, cat, base64
b:
Bandit Levels 0-10: SSH, ls, find, cat, base64

 Summary

Bandit is a text-only wargame with 60 levels and no account or VM — you SSH in and solve levels
in order. It is the ideal companion to Tier 0 because it forces you to use ls, find, cat,
grep, pipes and permissions until they stop being frightening.

How it works: connect, read the level description, find the password file for level N, and
read it. The passwords are generated from the previous level's flag, so you cannot skip.

bash
ssh bandit0@bandit.labs.overthewire.org -p 2220


 What levels 0-10 actually drill

| Levels | Skill |
|---|---|
| 0-3 | ls, find, cat, hidden files, absolute vs relative paths |
| 4-6 | ls -la, reading /etc/passwd, more/cat with hidden directories |
| 7-8 | find with -readable, hidden directories, permissions |
| 9-10 | strings, grep, find -exec, base64 decoding |

 Level notes

Level 0 — find and read. The flag is in a file in the home directory.

bash
ls -la
cat readme


Level 1 — the file is hidden. Nothing shows with plain ls.

bash
ls -a           -a = all, including dotfiles
cat -


Level 2 — hidden files, directories and somewhere else.

bash
ls -la
cat ./-         read a file whose name s

t: Bandit Levels 11-20: git, more encoding, pipes
b:
Bandit Levels 11-20: git, more encoding, pipes, /etc/shadow

 Summary

Levels 11-20 introduce git finding a stashed or deleted password, more encoding work,
/etc/passwd and /etc/shadow parsing, and pipes. The theme is reading data from places a
first-time user does not look: repositories, shadow files, and process output.

 Level notes

Level 11 — git has the password in its history.

bash
ls -la
cat .git/config
git log --oneline --all
git show                  the commit content
git log -p --all          every commit WITH its diff
cat .git/logs/HEAD        raw reflog, sometimes more revealing


The lesson: a .git directory is a complete history of the project, including things later
deleted. On a web target, an exposed .git hands over the source. This is exactly the
misconfiguration class from ms-04.

Level 12 — the port is in the gzipped git pack.

bash
ls -la
zcat .git/objects/pack/.pack.gz | strings | grep port


zcat or gunzip -c decompresses to stdout, so it pipes. Compressed data is just more data.

Level 13 — SSH key permission issues.

bash
ls -la
chmod 600 idrsa
ssh-keygen -y -f idrsa       derive the public key without logging in
ssh bandit13@localhost -i idrsa
chmod 644

t: Bandit Levels 21-29: su, cron, setuid, pipes and redirects
b:
Bandit Levels 21-29: su, cron, permissions, SUID, shell scripts

 Summary

Levels 21-29 are where Bandit stops being about find and starts being about privileges:
who can do what, which files a less-privileged user can abuse, and how a script or a cron job
becomes an escalation path. This is a direct preview of Tier 1 linux-privesc-doctrine.

The single idea across all nine levels: a process that runs as root but reads or executes
something a normal user can influence is a privilege escalation waiting to happen.

 Level notes

Level 21 — su and privileges.

bash
ls -la

 Summary

Three protocols you will see in every capture. Each has a distinctive shape, and each has a

 Summary

Every web vulnerability in this tier is a consequence of how HTTP works — or, more precisely, of
what a server must guess when a request is ambiguous. Before SQL injection or request
smuggling, you need the raw request in your head.

PortSwigger Academy's first topic is this foundation, and it is the note that makes
ps-08 request smuggling legible: smuggling exists because two HTTP implementations
disagree about where one request ends and the next begins.

 The request, byte by byte

http

Host: lab.internal:8080
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept: text/html
Cookie: session=abc123
Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz
X-Forwarded-For: 192.168.1.5

  HEADERS        KEY: VALUE, colon-space, CRLF each

SQL Injection and Blind SQLi

 Summary

SQL injection is the canonical example of ps-01's model: a string crosses from your input
into the SQL parser, and the two disagree about what the string is. Concatenation makes you a
participant in the query language.

The lecture's structure matters more than the payloads: how do you decide, from outside, what
you are looking at? That is the whole difficulty, and it is what separates blind from
non-blind.

 Companion to cs161-07's web taxonomy and atb-04 AD injection. This
 note is the mechanics and the decision tree.

 Why concatenation is the bug

sql
-- VULNERABLE: the value becomes part of the query language
SELECT  FROM users WHERE name = '$name'

-- name = ' OR 1=1 --      -  the quote closes the string, the rest is SQL
-- 1=1 is always true, -- comments out the trailing quote

-- SAFE: the value can never alter the structure
PREPARE stmt FROM 'SELECT  FROM users WHERE name = ?';
EXECUTE stmt USING @name;


Parameterisation is not escaping. It works because the database
receives the value and the query as separate inputs and does not
re-interpret the value. Escaping is a best-effort approximation of that,
and it fails when you forget,

Cross-Site Scripting and DOM XSS

 Summary

XSS is ps-01's model with the roles reversed: the server produces a string containing your
data, and the browser's parser treats it as markup. The bug is a disagreement between what
the server meant and what the browser did.

The critical insight from PortSwigger's framing is that the output context determines the
defence. <script is the vulnerability everyone looks for; it is one of at least eight.

 The three types

text
  REFLECTED   your input comes back in the response to your own request
              - needs a victim to click a crafted link
              - phishing-grade, easy to spot, usually patched first

  STORED      your input is saved and served to OTHER users
              - no victim interaction needed beyond visiting the page
              - session theft at scale, worms Samy, defacement
              - the highest severity of the three

  DOM         the payload never reaches the server; it executes in JS
              - source and sink are both in the page
              - invisible to server-side WAFs and to server logs
              - needs document.write/innerHTML/eval/location

All three of these are the same bug in different clothing: a string that names a resource
crosses from your input into a component that resolves names — a filesystem, a template

 Path traversal

text
  /download?file=report.pdf          - /home/www/report.pdf
  /download?file=../../etc/passwd    - /etc/passwd


 Encoding, and why it is always the reason

  WHAT THE STRING CONTAINS     WHAT EACH LAYER DECODES IT TO
  --------------------------   -------------------------------
  ../../etc/passwd             itself
  ..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd       after 1 URL decode
  ..%252f..%252fetc%252fpasswd after 2 URL decodes
  ..%c0%af..%c0%af             overlong UTF-8 legacy

The framing that matters: a session mechanism has exactly two trust
decisions to get right — is the token authentic, and is it valid for
this request. Everything here is one of those two being wrong.

Everything in ps-02 through ps-08 is a parsing bug: two components disagree about what a

The difficulty is that there is no oracle. A race condition has no

Collision Resistance and Hash Functions

 Summary

A hash function compresses an arbitrary input to a fixed output. For security, the property that
matters is not "it is hard to reverse" but collision resistance — and that property has a
specific meaning that determines which hashes are still usable and which are catastrophically
broken.

The course's framing: the hash function is the primitive behind signatures, commitments, git,
and blockchain. Breaking it breaks all of them at once.

 The three properties, precisely

text
  PREIMAGE RESISTANCE
    given hx, finding ANY x with hx = hx is hard.

  SECOND-PREIMAGE RESISTANCE
    given x, finding y != x with hy = hx is hard.

  COLLISION RESISTANCE
    finding ANY x != y with hx = hy is hard.

  COLLISION RESISTANCE  =  SECOND-PREIMAGE RESISTANCE  =  PREIMAGE RESISTANCE

  The reverse implications do not hold, and the gap is why MD5 survives
  in places where SHA-1 does not:

    signature / git / blockchain : needs COLLISION resistance  - broken
    password hashing             : needs PREIMAGE resistance   - still fine
    session token generation     : needs PREIMAGE resistance   - still fine
    file integrity               : ne

padding rather than on the mathematics. The math has held for 50 years; the encodings around it

insecurity, then PKCS1 v1.5, then OAEP, then the padding oracles that

 Summary

TCM Security's Practical Ethical Hacking is the only course in Tier 3 about process rather than
mechanism. Every other lecture in this tier teaches how something breaks. This one teaches how
to decide what to break, on whom, in what order, and how to prove you stayed inside the line
the whole time.

That ordering is the lesson. A pentest is not "hacking". It is a controlled experiment with a
written hypothesis, a defined blast radius, and a defensible record. An engagement that succeeds
technically and violates scope legally is a failed engagement.

 This note is the spine of the tier. Every later note in AEGIS that touches a target
 assumes you have read it. docs/RULES-OF-ENGAGEMENT.md in this repo is the
 application of it to your own labs.

 The engagement process

text
  1. RULES OF ENGAGEMENT   what you may touch, when, how hard, who to call
  2. SCOPING               which systems, which addresses, which time window
  3. RECON                 passive, then active; build a map
  4. ENUMERATION           services, versions, vulns; build a list
  5. EXPLOITATION          prove access; do not gold-plate
  6. P

Passive Reconnaissance and OSINT Collection

 Summary

The first stage of an engagement is to build a picture of the target without touching it.
Passive recon is what you can learn from data that already exists — DNS records, certificate
transparency logs, public code, breach corpora, job ads, documents, and the archive of the web.

The discipline point: passive recon has no footprint on the target. Nothing logs it,
nothing alerts, nothing gets rate-limited. That is why it happens first and why it is free.

 Companion to ccna-01/ccnad-01 for the protocol mechanics of what you
 are reading. This note is about the sources and how to weigh them.

 The sources, ranked by yield

|---|---|---|

| DNS records | A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, SPF, DMARC | free, no contact |
| ASN / WHOIS | Netblocks, hosting, ownership | free |
| Historical DNS / Wayback | Retired hosts, forgotten subdomains | free |
| Search engines | Docs, configs, credentials, error pages | free |
| Public code search | Credentials, keys, config files, endpoints | free |
| Breach corpora | Which

Active Reconnaissance and Network Scanning

 Summary

Active recon is where passive recon stops paying: you send packets to the target and observe
what answers. It is the first stage that leaves a trace — logs, IDS alerts, and sometimes a
ticket from the client's SOC.

The engineering content of this lecture is not "type nmap". It is: what does a port scan
actually learn, what does it cost, and what can you infer from a port that is closed, filtered,
or absent?

 Companion to ccnad-02 TCP/IP security problems and cs161-06
 firewalls. This note is the operational craft.

 What a port state tells you

text
  OPEN       - something accepted the connection. A service is there.
  CLOSED     - the host sent RST / ICMP unreachable. Nothing listening,
                but the host is ALIVE and reachable.
  FILTERED   - no response at all. Either a firewall dropped it, or the
                host is down, or the route is black-holed.
  open|filtered  UDP - no response either way; UDP has no handshake,
                          so this state is normal and nearly useless.


The genuinely useful inference: a filtered TCP port with every other
port closed is a strong signal that a firewall exist

Initial Access and Exploitation Basics

 Summary

Initial access is the moment a vulnerability becomes a foothold. This lecture covers the
discipline of choosing an exploit, proving access minimally, and — critically — stopping as
soon as you have what you need.

The most common failure mode for beginners is not inability to exploit; it is
inability to stop. A pentest that turns into an unsupervised takeover of the
client's environment is a failed engagement even if everything worked.

 Companion to ex-01..ex-06 the technical depth and cs161-04 the
 reasoning about chain construction. This note is the operational judgement.

 The decision, in order

text
  1. Is the target in scope and reachable?      tcm-01, tcm-03
  2. Does the vulnerability have a known fix?   if yes: report, do not exploit
  3. Is exploitation explicitly permitted?     ROE, not your judgement
  4. What is the SMALLEST proof?
  5. What is the blast radius of the technique?
  6. What is my stop condition?


Step 2 matters more than beginners expect. If a patch exists, the
finding is "this host is unpatched" and the proof is nmap -sV output.
Exploiting it proves nothing extra and creates risk. Reserve exploitation

Post-Exploitation and Privilege Escalation

 Summary

Post-exploitation answers a single question: what does this access actually give me? A shell
is a capability. A finding is an impact. This lecture is the translation step, and it is where
most of the value in a pentest report is produced.

The discipline is restraint. The instinct after gaining access is to go
further; the professional behaviour is to go exactly far enough to name the
impact, and then stop.

 Companion to cs161-05 privilege separation, the design side. This note
 is the offensive side, applied to a live Linux host you own.

 The post-exploitation loop

text
  1. ORIENT        who am I, where am I, what is this box?
  2. LOCALISE      enumerate users, groups, sudo rights, services
  3. EXPLOIT       escalate from current to root, minimally
  4. IMPACT        what does root on this box mean for the business?
  5. RESET         note what you changed, and change it back


Step 5 is the one nobody teaches and the one that saves you a call.

Pivoting and Internal Network Movement

 Summary

Pivoting is using one compromised host to reach networks you could not otherwise reach. It is
where engagements either become very valuable or very dangerous, because a pivot is the point
at which the blast radius grows by an order of magnitude.

The lecture's core discipline: every pivot is a new authorisation question. "I have a shell"
was never permission to scan the internal network.

 Companion to ccnad-01 routing and segmentation and atb-01

 Why pivot at all

text
  - segmentation worked, and the only way past it is a foothold
  - internal-only services AD, databases, management consoles
  - trust relationships: compromising a web server may reach an app server
  - the objective is behind a different firewall

  But also:
  - the perimeter IS the security boundary, and a flat network means the
    perimeter is the only defence. Proving that is the whole finding.


That last point is the one that belongs in the report. Pivoting without
hitting an authorisation boundary is itself the critical finding — it
proves segmentation does not exist.

The report is the deliverable. Everything before it is preparation; everything after it is
remediation. A technically successful engagement with an unusable report has failed the client.

The lecture's argument is that most of the value of a pentest arrives in the writing: the
technical part is a prerequisite for a report that changes decisions, and nothing else.

 This is the closing note of Tier 3, and it closes the loop with tcm-01:
 the ROE said what you would do; the report proves you did exactly that

  - an executive:      "what is the risk, what do we do, what does it cost?"
  - a manager:         "who owns this, when will it be fixed, do we accept risk?"
