Wireshark's CLI. Scriptable capture analysis - how you process a large pcap without opening a GUI.
Read and write raw TCP/UDP. The Swiss army knife for banners, listeners and reverse shells.
A connection where the target dials back to you, bypassing inbound filtering. The standard post-exploitation primitive.
Listening without transmitting. Invisible to the target but only works where you already have a legitimate position.
Each process gets its own address space, randomly based. Breaks the assumption that code lives at a fixed address.
Randomising stack, heap and library base addresses to defeat hardcoded addresses in exploits.
The per-function region of stack holding locals, saved registers and the return address. The target of classic stack smashing.

t: RSP / RBP and the Frame Pointer
b: RSP points at the current top of stack; RBP walks the frame chain. The map you draw before writing any payload.
The ABI rules for passing arguments, saving registers and returning. x86-64 System V is the one you will meet on Linux.
The small fast CPU storage. RAX, RDI, RSI and the carry flag carry most exploit payload meaning on x86-64.
Writing outside intended bounds. The root cause of most remote code execution for four decades.
Writing more bytes than a fixed buffer can hold, overwriting adjacent memory - typically the return address.
Overflowing the stack buffer to control the saved return address and redirect execution.
Corrupting heap allocator metadata for arbitrary read/write. Harder, and the source of most modern RCE chains.
Referencing memory after it was freed. Still one of the most common memory-safety bug classes in the wild.
A pointer to freed or unmapped memory. Use-after-free and type confusion are both flavours of it.
glibc's per-thread cache in front of the heap. Understanding it explains modern heap exploitation technique.
Chunk headers and free-list pointers stored inline in heap memory - the overwrite target in heap attacks.
Passing attacker-controlled data to printf-family functions, leaking memory or writing to arbitrary addresses.
Format-string functions. Their % specifiers are a read/write primitive when the format string itself is controllable.
Arithmetic wrapping past a type's bounds, leading to undersized allocations. Subtle and heavily exploited.
Silently dropping high-order bits on narrowing conversion - the bug behind many length-check bypasses.
A secret value placed between locals and the return address. Corrupt it and the program aborts before returning.
The glibc handler invoked when a canary check fails. Its presence in a binary tells you the mitigation is compiled in.
Non-executable stack and heap, forcing return-to-libc or ROP instead of injected shellcode.
Position-Independent Executable - the binary itself loads at a random base, defeating hardcoded code addresses.
Checking which mitigations a binary has: NX, PIE, canaries, RELRO, CET. Determines which technique you must use.
Makes the GOT read-only after relocation. Full RELRO plus PIE closes the GOT-overwrite route.
Overwriting a resolved library function pointer in the GOT to redirect a call. The classic ret2libc primitive.
Symbol resolution on first call, creating the writable GOT entries that ret2libc targets.
Chaining existing library calls instead of injecting shellcode, working around NX.
Building an execution chain from short instruction sequences already in the binary. The modern exploitation primitive.
Instruction endings you can jump to. Finding and chaining them is what a modern exploit actually is.
Machine code intended to run directly. Blocked by NX in most modern binaries, but still the clearest way to learn the ISA.
Leaking an address to defeat ASLR. Usually the second stage of a modern exploit chain.
Calling puts on a GOT entry to print a real libc address, then computing the base.
Escalating from a kernel bug to root. Dirty Pipe and friends show the pattern: reach a function pointer, control it, copy controlled data.
A Linux kernel pipe-flag flaw giving arbitrary page-cache write as root. The canonical modern kernel exploit walkthrough.
The public catalogue entry for a vulnerability: affected versions, references, CVSS score. The shared vocabulary of the field.
Splitting a privileged monitor from unprivileged userland so a compromise is contained. MIT 6.858's core theme.
Confining a process's capabilities: seccomp, namespaces, cgroups, containers.
The Linux primitives containers are built from. Shared-kernel isolation, and shared-kernel risk.
Breaking out of a container via privileged mounts, capabilities or kernel bugs. Why containers are not a security boundary on their own.
Allowlisting the syscalls a process may make. A direct expression of least privilege at the kernel boundary.
Hardware-isolated regions whose memory is encrypted and whose entry points are measured. Trust in hardware instead of process isolation.
Timing, cache and rollback attacks against trusted execution. Shows that isolation and trust are different problems.
Leaking secrets through observable side effects - timing, cache state, power - rather than through data.
Inferring secrets from how long operations take. Spectre and the cache-timing literature made this mainstream.
Out-of-order execution past a bounds check; Spectre/Meltdown turned it into a universal memory disclosure primitive.
Writing comparisons and crypto so timing does not depend on secret data. The defensive answer to side channels.
Concealment by intercepting the kernel's own view of the system - the hardest detection problem there is.
Recovering what a binary does from the artefact alone, without source. The core offensive discipline.
Machine code translated back into assembly. You will read more of this than C.
Examining the binary without running it - headers, strings, symbols, cross-references.
Running the binary and observing behaviour - debuggers, strace, tracing. Usually faster to insight than static work.
The debugger. Breakpoints, register inspection, memory examination - the single most valuable offensive tool after the shell.
Pausing at an address or on a memory change. Software INT3 breakpoints and the hardware breakpoints are worth knowing both of.
ptrace self-attach, timing checks, signal handlers. You will meet it in CTF reversing.
The syscall that grants one process control over another - how debuggers work, and how code detects them.
The executable container formats on Linux and Windows. Headers, sections and the entry point live here.
Inspecting a binary's mitigations to choose the right exploitation technique.
Extracting printable sequences from a binary. Fastest first look; offsets in the string table become your search anchors in a debugger.
Carving embedded filesystems and firmware out of firmware images. The entry point to IoT and embedded research.
Software baked into devices. Frequently unpatched, and a favourite target in CTF and bug bounty alike.
Half of reverse engineering is simply reading well-written code in another language.
Scriptable reverse engineering from the terminal, with a decompiler in the pro version.
NSA's free decompiler and disassembler. The standard for static analysis of native code.
Exploring program paths symbolically instead of by hand to find inputs that reach a target state. MIT 6.858's lecture 10.
Throwing malformed input at a program to find crashes automatically. AFL and its descendants.
Runtime hooking of functions and objects in a live process - how you bypass anti-debug and instrument mobile targets.
Writing and reading simple assembly: mov, lea, call, ret, syscalls. The prerequisite for most of this tier.
scheme, userinfo, host, port, path, query, fragment. Almost every web vulnerability is a parsing disagreement between two implementations.
Method, target, version, headers, body. The most attacked protocol you will ever read.
Status, headers, body. Status codes and headers leak behaviour and misconfiguration.
Injecting extra headers or splitting responses via newline handling. Classic bug, still present.
Desynchronising how a front-end proxy and back-end server parse the same request stream - CL.TE and TE.CL variants.
Two systems disagreeing on how to interpret the same bytes. The root cause behind smuggling, SSRF bypass and cache poisoning.
Forward proxies relay client requests; reverse proxies front a backend. TLS termination usually happens here.
Burp or mitmproxy positioned between client and server so every request can be inspected and modified.
The standard web testing proxy. Repeater, Intruder, Scanner - and the single best tool for learning HTTP by hand.
Same-origin policy, trust boundaries and the privileges the browser grants a page.
Browsers restrict cross-origin reads by default. Nearly every CORS problem and many XSS chains involve defeating it.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing - the mechanism that relaxes SOP by returning Access-Control-* headers.
Default credentials, verbose errors, directory listing, cloud storage left public. OWASP's most common category.
Server-side session identifiers, their flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), and why cookie parsing is a prime injection point.
Attacker sets or steals the session identifier so the victim's authenticated traffic runs on it.
Cross-site request forgery: borrowing the victim's ambient cookie authority to issue authenticated requests.
Referer checks, synchroniser tokens and SameSite cookies - three ways to blunt CSRF.
Injecting script that runs in another user's origin. Stored, reflected and DOM-based.
The weaker sibling of XSS: injecting markup rather than script, still useful for phishing and form tampering.
Context-aware escaping applied at output time. The actual defence against XSS.
A response header declaring which script sources are allowed. A strong second line of defence against XSS.
Injecting SQL syntax through unsanitised input to alter the query the application intends to run.
Stored input that is only dangerous when reused in a later query. Hard to spot, frequently present.
Abusing document-store query operators ($ne, $gt, $where) when user input is passed straight into a query object.
Separating code from data so input can never alter query structure. The real fix for injection.
Relational and document stores, their query languages, and the trust boundary between application and data.
Extracting schema, table names and rows from a reachable database during an authorised test.
Feeding attacker-controlled data to an object mapper that instantiates arbitrary classes. RCE in most languages.
Chaining existing harmless methods into a dangerous sequence - the same idea as ROP, applied to object graphs.
Java's native object serialisation, long notorious for unauthenticated RCE. Replaced by safer formats in modern stacks.
Making the server issue a request to a resource you cannot reach directly - metadata services, internal admin panels.
The 169.254.169.254 endpoint on cloud VMs that hands out credentials. The canonical SSRF payoff.
AWS/GCP/Azure service model. Misconfigured storage and IAM are consistently high-severity findings.
Who may do what, in the cloud and in the enterprise directory.
Changing an object identifier to reach another user's data. Still the web's most common high-severity bug.
Authentication (who) then authorization (what). Missing object-level checks are where it breaks.
Server-side enforcement that the current principal may act on the requested resource.
XML External Entity injection - abusing the XML parser to read local files or make outbound requests.
DTDs, external entities and the parser settings that make them dangerous.
Using ../ or encoding tricks to escape the intended directory. Born directly from Unix path semantics.
Including arbitrary local files through a parameter, often to read source and defeat 'black box' testing.
Uploading executable content - shells, polyglots, or files processed unsafely by a parser.
Tricking a user into clicking a transparent overlay in a frame. Fixed with X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors.
Compact signed claims. The classic flaws are alg=none, key confusion, and trusting unverified claims.
Checking signature, issuer, audience and expiry - every JWT flaw is a missing check here.
The industry list of web risk categories. The standard vocabulary for a web pentest report.
Fuzzing paths, parameters and headers. The discovery step before any targeted attack.
Brute-forcing paths with wordlists. Where legacy admin panels are found.
Passive collection, then active enumeration, then mapping the attack surface before exploitation.
Discovering the full external hostname list of a target - the modern perimeter.
Public logs of issued TLS certificates - a free, reliable subdomain discovery source.
subfinder, amass and friends aggregate CT logs and passive sources without touching the target.
Automated SQL injection testing and extraction. Effective, and a last resort - manual testing teaches you more.
A cipher conceals using a key; an encoding does not. Checking which you are actually facing is step one of every crypto challenge.
One shared key encrypts and decrypts. Fast, and the right tool for bulk data. AES is the standard.
The block cipher standard, with a 128-bit block and 128/192/256-bit keys. Its weakness is never the cipher, it is the mode.
How a block cipher is applied: ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM. Using AES in ECB is a bug, not a style choice.
Encrypts each block independently, so patterns in the plaintext survive. Immediately recognisable in a ciphertext.
An attacker who can distinguish padding errors from other errors decrypts CBC ciphertext without the key. The most famous crypto attack.
The predictable padding scheme behind CBC padding oracles. Its structure is the vulnerability.
Using any observable difference - error message, timing, status code - to learn a secret. A general attack pattern.
A public key encrypts, a private key decrypts (or signs). Solves key distribution; roughly 1000x slower than symmetric.
Trapdoor permutation whose security rests on factoring. Broken by shared or small-prime moduli and by textbook padding.
Equivalent security with far smaller keys - the basis of modern TLS and most cryptocurrency.
Proving a message came from a keyholder without revealing it. Authentication, not secrecy.
Sign with a private key, verify with a public key. The backbone of code signing, JWTs and certificates.
Agreeing a shared secret over an insecure channel. Ephemeral DH is what modern TLS uses.
Stripping a connection to a weaker protocol or cipher suite. Pure key-exchange misuse, still highly effective.
A fixed-length one-way function. Integrity and password storage - note the very different requirements.
Finding two inputs with the same hash. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken here, which breaks signatures and file integrity.
MD5 and SHA-1. Collision-broken, and still present everywhere. Always a finding in an audit.
Per-password random data defeating precomputation. It goes in the hash, not next to it.
A unique-per-message value. Never reuse one with the same key in CTR/GCM - that is catastrophic, not theoretical.
Real randomness is a hardware property. `/dev/urandom` and RDRAND/RDSEED are the sources; VMs can weaken them.
Good keys come from a CSPRNG. Predictable keys make strong ciphers irrelevant - Kerberoasting is exactly this bug.
Deliberately slow, salted algorithms: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2. Never a bare fast hash.
Precomputed hash-to-password chains. Defeated by a salt, and memory-hungry - exactly why salts exist.
Dictionary word + numeric suffix, the shape of almost every real password. Rules in hashcat express them.
Recovering a plaintext from a hash. Only legitimate against your own hashes and CTF challenges.
The two great crackers. john is flexible with formats; hashcat is fast with GPU and rule engines.
Identifying a hash by its prefix so you pick the right cracking mode. Cheap, and constantly needed.
The protocol that authenticates a server, negotiates keys, and encrypts the channel. Three properties, three failure modes.
ClientHello, ServerHello, certificate verification, key agreement, finished. Read it in Wireshark and the whole picture lands.
Binding a public key to an identity, signed by an issuer. The trust chain is the whole point.
Certificate authorities, the trust store, revocation. The machinery that makes certificate fraud possible and detectable.
Downgrading a connection or stripping the scheme to defeat encryption in transit.
The directory service holding Windows domain identity, policy and machines. The map of a large enterprise network.
The protocol AD exposes. Knowing the query syntax and the default naming context is what makes enumeration productive.
Injecting filter syntax into an LDAP query. Same class of bug as SQL injection, different grammar.
Ticket-based authentication: AS-REQ/TGT for authentication, TGS-REQ/service ticket for access. Understanding it explains most AD attacks.
The AD identity a service runs as. Discoverable by anyone who can enumerate the domain, and crackable when the service password is weak.
Requesting service tickets for all SPNs and cracking them offline. No alerting, no lockouts.
Accounts with no pre-authentication required let you request a crackable TGT for anyone.
Authenticating with the NTLM hash directly - no need to ever recover the plaintext.
Windows LAN authentication. Hash-based, replayable, and still enabled almost everywhere for legacy reasons.
Capturing and relaying an authentication to a different service. Needs SMB signing and EPA turned off.
Microsoft's defence against relay. When disabled, relay attacks become trivial.
Reusing a captured Kerberos ticket to authenticate as that principal without the key.
Forging tickets with the KRBTGT or service key - domain admin equivalent, requires krbtgt hash access.
Abusing trust relationships between domains or forests - the path from one org to its parent.
ldapsearch, BloodHound, and reading group memberships to find the shortest path to Domain Admin.
Building the full picture: users, groups, hosts, services, shares. 80% of a pentest is this step.
Mapping AD as a graph of users, groups and sessions to find the shortest privilege path.
Modelling every path from your foothold to the crown jewels, then closing them in order of reachability.
Windows file and print sharing. Shares are the most common initial access vector on internal networks.
Enumerating SMB shares and permissions from Kali - often the first credential found on an internal box.
Windows remote execution, used by Impacket's psexec and wmiexec to move laterally with credentials.
Creating a service on a remote host to execute a payload as SYSTEM. The classic lateral movement primitive.
Compromising additional hosts after the first. Pivoting, credential reuse and trust relationships drive it.
Using one compromised host as a network hop to reach otherwise unreachable segments.
Wrapping traffic in another protocol (SSH -L/-R, SOCKS) to cross a segmentation boundary.
Routing arbitrary tools through a SOCKS proxy - so nmap and netcat can travel the tunnel.
TCP/UDP tunnelling over HTTP or WebSocket - useful when only port 80/443 is reachable.
C2 tunnelling over common web ports to blend with normal traffic. Always in an authorised lab context.
Credential extraction from LSASS memory - hashes, tickets, plaintext. The tool every Windows defender must know.
Dumping the LSASS process memory to recover credentials. Rootkit-level tradecraft, heavily monitored.
MITRE ATT&CK T1003 family - extracting stored credentials from a compromised host.
Credentials leaking via logs, environment variables, config files or shell history. Boring and extremely effective.
Service misconfigurations, unquoted service paths, token abuse, AlwaysInstallElevated, weak ACLs.
Abusing GPO edit rights or Group Policy Preferences to plant scheduled tasks or local admins across a whole OU.
Automated Linux privilege escalation enumeration - a checklist of the misconfigurations from this tier.
Python implementations of Windows protocols - secretsdump, psexec, wmiexec, ntlmrelay. The Kali operator's best friend.
Bit-for-bit copying a disk to an image file. The first step of any disk investigation.
Documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence and when. Without it, findings are inadmissible.
SHA-256 the image before analysis and after, proving nothing changed during examination.
Recovering files by signature rather than by directory entry - recovers deleted data with no filesystem structure.
Header byte patterns that identify a file type regardless of its name. The basis of carving and format identification.
Signature-based carving tools shipped with Kali. First responders' default.
Memory forensics framework - process listing, network connections, injected code, from a RAM image.
RAM holds the live truth: running processes, decrypted data, network state, injected shellcode that never touches disk.
Classic signs of hollowing and reflective loading: private RWX pages, hollowed modules, missing on-disk modules.
Merging filesystem, registry and log timestamps into one sequence to reconstruct an attacker's dwell time.
MFT times, $LogFile, journal entries - each has quirks. Getting time normalisation wrong invalidates a timeline.
Auth logs, syslog, Windows event IDs. Reading them the way an attacker leaves them - the defender's core skill.
Open-source disk analysis suite used widely in IR engagements and CTF challenges.
Blue-team CTF platforms with realistic disk/memory/pcap challenges - the cheapest way to practise IR.
Pattern language for identifying malware families and interesting byte sequences. Detection engineering's core tool.
Vendor-neutral log detection rules, convertible to nearly any SIEM query format. Pairs with YARA.
Static first: hashes, strings, imports, signatures. Dynamic second, in a sandbox, only when justified.
VM/sandbox detection, debugger checks, timing and environment fingerprinting to frustrate analysts.
Log wiping, timestomping, secure deletion, steganography, rootkits. Understanding it shapes your detection strategy.
Hiding data inside apparently innocuous carriers (images, audio). Found by steghide and strings analysis.
Reading and stripping document metadata - GPS coordinates, editing software, usernames. A classic OSINT and IR source.
Signature-based NIDS. Seeing your traffic as a rule author teaches you what detection actually costs.
Authenticated scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS) matching live services to CVE data. In Nikus, nikto and searchsploit terms.
Kali's web server vulnerability scanner. Good recon, noisy signatures - always read the output critically.
Offline database of exploits and papers shipped with Kali. Search by product and version - your best starting point.
Intelligence gathered from publicly available sources, legally and ethically collected. The first phase of most engagements.
A taxonomy linking techniques to the sources that support them. Use it as a checklist, not a script.
Collecting target information without touching their infrastructure. Always safe, always legal, often sufficient.
The Admiralty Code: rating source reliability and information credibility separately. Pre you believing a single source.
Document and file metadata as an intelligence source - EXIF GPS, document properties, revision history.
Confirming a finding is genuinely exposed before reporting it - the line between research and noise.
Turning collected indicators into actionable context about who, why and how. Attribution with discipline.
Building a complete profile of a target's people, technology and attack surface before engagement begins.
Manipulating human trust rather than technical controls. Requires explicit written authorisation, always.
Deceptive messages to harvest credentials or deliver payloads. Blue-team analysis is always legitimate; simulation needs authorisation.
Reading Authentication-Results, SPF, DKIM, DMARC and Received chains to establish authenticity.
Forging From/Reply-To/Return-Path. SPF/DKIM/DMARC exist because of it; reading them is basic tradecraft.
SMTP for sending, IMAP/POP3 for retrieval, and the auth mechanisms each uses.
A fabricated but plausible scenario used to justify a request for information or access.
Voice and SMS variants of phishing. Awareness training and reporting are the defensive answers.
Competitive security exercises where you capture flags to prove a skill. The most efficient way to retain what you study.
The proof token (flag{...}, AEGIS{...}) you submit on completion. Record each solved challenge and what taught you.
A written record of how you solved a challenge. Writing one is what turns a lucky solve into retained knowledge.
Guided beginner-friendly rooms, many explicitly authorised for practice. Ideal for Tier 0-2 consolidation.
Proving-grounds style machines and labs. Closest to real engagement difficulty once past the easy tier.
Free competitive platforms from Carnegie Mellon and Arizona State, with beginner and collegiate tracks.
A zero-setup, text-based Linux and security gauntlet. The perfect Tier 0 companion - run entirely in the terminal.
Command-line challenges that build real fluency in grep, awk, sed and quoting. The fastest path from beginner to competent.
A binary you must understand to solve. Cracking the key-check logic is the exercise.
Exploit a vulnerability under CTF constraints, usually with source provided and protections limited.
Partial protections in challenge binaries (canary only, no PIE, RELRO off) that steer your technique.
Break a cipher, encoding or signature scheme. Usually small-numbers, ECB reuse, or weak randomness.
Predictable seeds, duplicate nonces, or reused IVs. The most common real-world crypto break.
Break an intentionally vulnerable web app. Source usually given to teach the pattern.
Analyse a pcap, disk or memory image for a flag. Teaches triage and the artefacts of each attack class.
Find a publicly available artefact that proves a fact about the target. Legitimate when scoped to public data.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals. The reason the glossary and self-test exist in AEGIS.
Promote each lecture's terminology into a review queue. Every term is a card, every card is a rerun.
Security is a vocabulary. Mastering the terms is not memorisation - it is being able to read the documentation.
hexdump, xxd, od - inspecting raw bytes. Where CTF files always hide something.
Turning manual process into repeatable scripts - the highest-leverage habit in security work.
Loops, conditionals, argument parsing and error handling for recon pipelines and evidence collection.
Chaining tools so output of one feeds the next - nmap into grep into a target list, tshark into jq.
Variables, control flow, functions, files, and modules - the scripting substrate for all of Kali's automation.
Writing raw TCP/UDP connections in Python - connect to a port, send a banner, script a scan.
The network mapper. Host discovery, port scanning, service fingerprinting and scripting - the first tool you reach for.
A modular exploitation framework. Metasploitable VMs exist precisely so you can practise on it legally.
Standardised modules for payload, encoding and evasion - a practical introduction to exploitation on a legal target.
Metasploit's post-exploitation agent: sessions, pivoting, keylogging, credential interaction.
The line between a lab and a crime. Written authorisation, or a platform that provides the target.
The written document defining what is permitted, when, and by whom. Non-negotiable before any testing.
Exactly which systems, IPs, techniques and time windows are authorised. The first section of any engagement paperwork.
Findings with evidence, risk, impact and remediation. The deliverable that makes the work matter.
How findings get prioritised. A critical in an unused system outranks a high in production.
An index or bound error of exactly one. Trivial to spot in source, still the most common bug class.
Unbounded C string functions. They copy until a null byte with no destination-size check - the textbook overflow primitive.
The bounded replacements. Note their own traps: no guaranteed null termination, and off-by-one destination sizing.
Checking a condition then acting on it later, with a gap attackers can win. Symlink swaps, file checks and ID races are all this.
Predictable temporary file or directory names, enabling symlink races against privileged processes.
The MMU translating virtual to physical addresses on demand. Every memory-safety bug is ultimately resolved here.
How many routers a packet may traverse before being dropped. The mechanism behind traceroute and a way to infer topology.
The libpcap capture format. Every sniffer writes one, and forensic tools read them as evidence.
Structuring tool output before use. Turn an API or tool response into clean fields you can act on.
Reaching protected functionality without valid credentials - via logic flaws, injection, or default credentials.
A rogue access point impersonating a legitimate one, capturing credentials or hijacking traffic.
Front-end infrastructure that distributes requests. Parsing disagreements here cause smuggling and cache issues.
Inspecting ELF headers, sections, symbols and disassembly from the command line. The first static-analysis tools you reach for.
Finding ROP gadgets in a binary. Automates the manual gadget hunt.
Kali's all-in-one ARP, Wi-Fi and BLE attack toolkit. Handy for learning MITM mechanics safely.
Classic in-suite MITM framework for switched networks - ARP poisoning plus credential sniffing.
Capturing cleartext authentication from traffic - FTP, Telnet, HTTP Basic, POP3. All still present on real networks.
Assessing wireless security: handshake capture, PMKID, rogue APs. Requires authorisation - only ever test your own or an authorised WLAN.
Multiplexer and relay for arbitrary sockets. Building reverse shells and bridging protocols are its commonest uses.
Content discovery tools with tuned wordlists and recursion. Finds legacy admin paths others miss.
Fast parallel host discovery. arp-scan resolves hosts to MAC addresses for L2 awareness.
Protocol fuzzer that can poison ARP, DHCP and STP. A research tool - authorised targets only.
Transforming shellcode or payloads to survive bad characters and evade signatures.
The media downloader used to pull public lecture captions for offline study. Installed cleanly with pipx.
Kali organises thousands of tools by category - recon, scanning, exploitation, forensics, reporting. Learn the categories; the tools change, the categories do not.
/usr/share/nmap, /usr/share/wordlists, /usr/share/seclists, /usr/share/metasploit-framework - where the payload data actually lives on disk.
The discovery data that makes brute-force practical: usernames, passwords, directories, SPN names. Kali ships SecLists.
Running guest OSes on a host hypervisor. Every practice lab, isolated target and snapshot workflow depends on it.
Freezing a VM state so an exercise can be repeated identically - essential for learning exploitation reliably.
Your own deliberately vulnerable infrastructure, on isolated networking, where testing is legal by construction.
The language exploitation is written in. Manual memory management, undefined behaviour and why the compiler lets you corrupt memory.
Many tasks progressing over time. Thread interleaving produces races, deadlocks and the desync bugs web smuggling exploits.
Operations that cannot be interrupted partway. The mitigation for races - and the source of deadlock when badly ordered.
Splitting a network so containment is real. The defensive control that pivoting exists to defeat.
The trust-on-first-use, spoofable and unencrypted properties baked into TCP/IP: IP spoofing, smurf, session hijacking, weak TCP sequence numbers.
Code that works exactly as written while doing the wrong thing - price manipulation, workflow skips, missing state checks. Invisible to scanners.
Officially sanctioned, intentionally vulnerable VMs for legal practice. The safest way to run a real exploitation exercise.
Kerberos, LDAP, SPNs, delegation and the practical enumeration-and-exploitation sequence that modern AD assessment follows.
